title: A transferable carbon-concentrating system for C3 staple crops

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a coordinated biological system that raises the concentration of carbon dioxide around Rubisco, the main carbon-fixing enzyme, in C3 staple crops such as rice and wheat. Its intended effect is to reduce photorespiratory losses and improve productive carbon fixation. The target is a functioning system that can be transferred between crops, rather than the expression of an individual enzyme associated with carbon concentration. This is the scientific framing supplied by the research and review; the retained source provides no inspectable scientific text establishing its implementation.

In this proposed design, carbon transport, enzyme activity, cellular organization and metabolism must work together. A system would need to deliver and retain elevated carbon dioxide near Rubisco while operating within the crop's energy and nutrient budget. A C4-pathway component, such as maize phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase, could be relevant to one implementation, but its presence alone would not establish coordinated carbon concentration, transferability or agronomic benefit. The concept remains broader than that particular component or implementation route.

significance.text: As a conditional impact assessment, a successful system would change how a major food crop supplies carbon dioxide to its carbon-fixing machinery. Sustained carbon concentration with reduced photorespiration could remove an important constraint on photosynthetic performance. Making that capability transferable would extend the achievement beyond a single engineered crop and create a reusable approach to crop improvement. The supplied review considers this rationale scientifically coherent, but the retained source does not substantiate the underlying physiological consequences.

Possible downstream benefits include greater harvested yield or improved output per unit of a limiting resource, provided the additional carbon fixation exceeds the system's operating costs and the crop converts the benefit into harvestable material. These outcomes require separate demonstrations: improved leaf photosynthesis does not by itself establish higher grain yield, better whole-season resource productivity or reliable performance across climates. Likewise, success in rice would not establish that the same design works in wheat or other C3 staples. The revolutionary potential lies in combining physiological function, crop transfer and agronomic value; none should be inferred solely from another.

missing_breakthrough.text: The proposed missing capability is an integrated, energetically effective carbon-concentrating mechanism in a C3 staple that can subsequently be adapted to another staple. The engineering problem is to coordinate carbon delivery with Rubisco activity, regulate the relevant enzymes in the plant, organize the participating processes in compatible cellular locations and integrate their metabolic demands with normal growth. Adding an active enzyme would address only part of that problem. These barriers are the research's proposed scientific framing, rather than requirements verified from the retained article.

Concrete questions for development include whether the engineered transport and metabolism can sustain a local carbon dioxide increase, whether that increase actually reduces photorespiration, and whether maintaining it imposes energy or nutrient costs that cancel the benefit. A transferable design must also accommodate differences between recipient crops instead of assuming that a construct effective in one plant will retain its regulation and performance in another. The supplied evidence cannot establish which of these barriers has already been overcome, or confirm that the entire capability remained absent as of 11 November 2026.

current_state.text: The supplied research reports a study attributed to Kuenzang Om, Rita Giuliani and colleagues, titled “Expression of maize PEPC in rice reveals a strategy for establishing a functional C4 CO2-concentrating mechanism,” reportedly published in Plant Physiology on 6 October 2026, with DOI 10.1093/plphys/kiag387. It associates that study with maize phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase expression in rice and with regulatory and metabolic constraints encountered in the plant. These are reported bibliographic details and findings in the supplied research, not independently verified publication metadata or demonstrated results in this assessment.

According to the supplied review, the retained artifact for the PubMed URL contains only a cookie-access notice. It contains no article-identifying content, abstract or scientific discussion. Consequently, describing the evidence as an abstract-only assessment would overstate what was available: neither the reported expression result nor the claimed regulatory and metabolic findings could be inspected. The source index records a saved artifact, but successful retention does not establish that the intended article content was captured.

The available material therefore establishes no inspectable demonstration of a complete carbon-concentrating mechanism, transfer between staples or field-yield improvement. It also supplies no contrary scientific evidence showing that the reported component result is false. Even if enzyme expression were verified, additional evidence would still be needed to determine whether coordinated carbon concentration, reduced photorespiration and agronomic benefits followed. Those distinctions concern what each result would establish, rather than a finding that the uninspected study failed those tests.

The supplied record contains no usable quantitative measurements of carbon concentration, photosynthetic gain, harvested yield, energy cost or nutrient demand. It also provides no substantive freshness record from which to assess the wider field through 11 November 2026. The reported October 2026 publication should therefore remain a research lead with unresolved findings, rather than a verified milestone or evidence that the proposed innovation has been achieved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: establish sustained carbon concentration around Rubisco in engineered rice, accompanied by reduced photorespiration under explicitly defined conditions. The evidence should distinguish the intended concentrating mechanism from component expression or a change in leaf performance alone. Appropriate comparisons should allow the observed effects to be attributed to the engineered system, and measurements should account for its energy and nutrient requirements. These are proposed criteria for a convincing demonstration, not established field standards.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained carbon concentration around Rubisco reduces photorespiration in rice

completion_criteria.text: Proposed transfer demonstration: reproduce the functional capability in another major C3 staple, documenting the adaptations required and the conditions in which it operates. Transfer should include evidence of carbon concentration and reduced photorespiration in the second crop, rather than gene expression alone. This would demonstrate transfer across the tested crops; it would not establish universal compatibility with all C3 plants.
completion_criteria.label: Carbon concentration reducing photorespiration transfers to another C3 staple

completion_criteria.text: Proposed agronomic demonstration: show substantial, repeatable gains in harvested yield or clearly defined resource productivity in independent field trials across a specified range of relevant climates. Trial plans should define in advance what counts as substantial, identify the resource denominator when claiming productivity gains, and report operating costs, variability and conditions in which the advantage disappears. Independent replication should establish that the benefit persists beyond the original experimental setting. Finite trials would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, not performance under every climate or farming system.
completion_criteria.label: Independent field trials reproduce substantial yield or resource productivity gains

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: AGR-01, “Cereal crops supplied predominantly by biological nitrogen fixation,” shares the challenge of integrating a complex biological capability into staple crops. Its central target is nitrogen supply, whereas AGR-02 targets carbon dioxide delivery to Rubisco. Their interaction could matter when evaluating nutrient requirements and crop productivity, but success in either capability would not establish the other.

Roster-based synthesis: AGR-03, “Reliable clonal seed reproduction across major hybrid crops,” concerns inheritance and reproduction, while AGR-07, “A general, rapid method for creating productive crops from wild plants,” concerns creating crops from wild starting material. Both intersect with the broader task of making engineered plant traits useful and reproducible. AGR-02 specifically requires a transferable photosynthetic function; it does not establish clonal seed production or a general domestication method.

Roster-based synthesis: AGR-04, “High-yield perennial versions of the major grain-crop portfolio,” and AGR-05, “Productive staple farming with seawater and a closed salt balance,” address different constraints on staple agriculture: perennial crop performance and saline production systems. Carbon concentration might eventually be combined with either, but it does not itself confer perennial growth, seawater tolerance or a closed salt balance. Any combined yield or resource benefit would need its own demonstration.

Roster-based synthesis: AGR-06, “Rapidly programmable, durable crop immunity,” overlaps through plant engineering but targets disease protection. AGR-08, “Economically accessible, end-to-end autonomous field farming,” targets the operation and economics of farming. Neither immune durability nor autonomous field operation follows from improved photosynthetic physiology; they remain separate innovations even where they could contribute to the same production system.

Roster-based synthesis: AGR-09, “Food crops that reliably build durable, additional soil carbon,” shares an interest in plant carbon flows. AGR-02 targets carbon concentration and productive fixation within the crop, whereas AGR-09 requires additional carbon to enter and remain in soil durably. Increased photosynthesis or harvested yield would not by itself demonstrate additional, persistent soil carbon storage.

unresolved_issues: The intended PubMed article's identity, authorship, publication date, DOI and scientific contents remain unverified because the retained artifact contains only a cookie-access notice.
The reported maize PEPC expression result and associated regulatory and metabolic constraints cannot be confirmed or characterized from the supplied evidence.
The supplied material cannot establish the wider field's demonstrated progress or whether the complete proposed capability remained missing as of 11 November 2026.
The physiological rationale and engineering requirements remain a coherent supplied framing without substantive source text available to support them here.

A concrete demonstration program still needs numerical definitions of substantial improvement, the selected resource-productivity measures, trial climates, acceptable operating costs and replication requirements.

brief.title: More efficient food crops with a transferable system
possible: Rice and wheat could capture carbon more efficiently with a biological system that concentrates carbon dioxide around Rubisco, the enzyme that captures carbon for growth. The system would reduce photorespiration, an energy-wasting reaction with oxygen, and could be adapted from one staple crop to another.
why: Farmers could harvest more grain or produce more food with the same water or nutrient supply. A reusable system could extend those benefits beyond a single engineered crop.

sources.who: Kuenzang Om, Rita Giuliani and colleagues
sources.showed: A maize carbon-capturing enzyme called PEPC worked in rice, but its activity inside plants was less than 2.1% of its activity in laboratory tests. Chemical changes that regulate its activity occurred mainly in darkness.
sources.quote: Both cDNAlines and gDNAlines showed higher PEPC activities than wild-type rice, but in planta activity was <2.1% of in vitro activity.
sources.cited_for: Putting a carbon-capturing enzyme into rice does not ensure that it works efficiently inside the plant.
sources.not_established: The study did not establish a complete system that concentrates carbon dioxide around Rubisco and reduces photorespiration.

sources.who: Chiara Baccolini, Stéphanie Arrivault, Florence Danila and colleagues
sources.showed: Engineered rice carried out all four core reactions of the C4 pathway, a biochemical cycle that concentrates carbon dioxide in plants such as maize.
sources.quote:
We demonstrate that these four core C
4
reactions are operating in rice, establishing the in vivo flux framework needed to progress towards a functional carbon-concentrating mechanism.
sources.cited_for: Several linked biochemical steps can operate in engineered rice.
sources.not_established: Activity through the cycle does not establish sustained carbon concentration, reduced photorespiration or higher harvested yield.

sources.who: Taiyu Chen, Marta Hojka and colleagues
sources.showed: The team built carboxysomes, protein compartments enclosing Rubisco, inside tobacco chloroplasts, where photosynthesis occurs. These supported photosynthesis and growth under elevated carbon dioxide.
sources.quote: Here, we generate morphologically correct carboxysomes in tobacco chloroplasts by transforming nine carboxysome genetic components derived from a proteobacterium.
sources.cited_for: Bacterial compartments for capturing carbon can be assembled and function inside a plant.
sources.not_established: Growth under elevated carbon dioxide does not establish a complete concentrating system operating in ordinary air or in staple crops.

sources.who: Benedict M. Long, Wei Yih Hee and colleagues
sources.showed: The team produced simplified carboxysomes enclosing bacterial Rubisco in tobacco chloroplasts. The plants grew using photosynthesis under elevated carbon dioxide.
sources.quote:
This minimal gene set produces carboxysomes, which encapsulate the introduced Rubisco and enable autotrophic growth at elevated CO
2
.
sources.cited_for: A reduced set of bacterial genes can build Rubisco-containing compartments inside a plant.
sources.not_established: Simplified compartments alone do not establish a functioning carbon-concentrating system.

shown: Chiara Baccolini and colleagues have demonstrated the core carbon-concentrating cycle’s reactions in rice. This advances beyond adding an isolated enzyme, but does not yet demonstrate that rice maintains extra carbon dioxide around Rubisco or loses less energy to photorespiration.

Taiyu Chen and colleagues demonstrated another route in tobacco: bacterial protein compartments that support photosynthesis under elevated carbon dioxide. Neither route yet establishes a transferable system with repeatable benefits in farmers’ fields.
missing: Rice needs an integrated system that sustains carbon concentration and reduces photorespiration without excessive energy or nutrient costs.
The functioning capability has yet to be demonstrated in another staple crop.
Independent field trials still need to reproduce substantial gains in harvested yield or output per unit of a defined resource across relevant climates.

milestones.label: Rice sustains carbon concentration and reduces photorespiration
milestones.explanation: Engineered rice would have to sustain extra carbon dioxide around Rubisco and reduce photorespiration under defined conditions, with energy and nutrient costs measured. This would establish that the integrated system works.

milestones.label: Another staple crop gains the same functioning capability
milestones.explanation: Another staple crop would have to sustain carbon concentration and reduce photorespiration, with required adaptations documented. This would establish transfer beyond rice.

milestones.label: Independent field trials reproduce substantial crop benefits
milestones.explanation: Independent field trials would have to reproduce substantial yield or defined resource-productivity gains across specified climates. This would establish practical value beyond the original experimental setting.

uncertain: The size of a gain that would count as substantial remains undefined.
It remains unclear which crops and climates could support the system without its energy and nutrient demands erasing the benefit.

page.title: Carbon-concentrating mechanisms in C3 staple crops
page.definition: An engineered carbon-concentrating mechanism (CCM) raises CO2 around Rubisco, the carbon-fixing enzyme, in C3 crops, whose first fixation product has three carbons. The same engineered core functions in at least two staples, reducing photorespiration, the carbon and energy loss following Rubisco's reaction with oxygen, and increasing harvested yield.

goal.need: Photorespiration reduces the efficiency of converting light into biomass in C3 crops by an estimated 20–50%, with the largest losses in hot, dry conditions. The C4 Rice Project reports that more than 3 billion people depend on rice. A CCM supplies CO2 to Rubisco to suppress its competing reaction with oxygen.

statements.quote: aims to improve photosynthetic efficiency in rice and thus to enhance crop yields.
We propose to enhance CO2 assimilation in crops
Finally, we transform our target food crops with the successful modifications to boost the yield of cowpea, cassava, rice, and soybeans.

completion.title: The same engineered CCM increases carbon fixation and harvested yield in two C3 staple crops.
completion.criterion: Peer-reviewed experiments establish that the same engineered CCM core, with crop-specific adaptations identified, functions in at least two C3 staple species. In each species, the complete mechanism elevates CO2 at Rubisco and reduces photorespiration relative to matched controls; field experiments establish increased harvested yield. Component expression, compartment assembly and pathway flux alone do not satisfy the test. No fixed percentage gain or trial size is stipulated.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; explicit fallback for cross-crop transfer.
completion.basis: Searched C4 Rice goals, RIPE translation objectives, BBSRC–NSF pyrenoid awards, USDA crop-readiness criteria, and CCM standards, prizes and cross-crop success criteria. No body defines completion for a transferable CCM across staple species. Two species is the minimum operational meaning of transfer; physiological function and field yield connect the programme goals without treating projected percentage gains as thresholds.

milestones.title: An introduced CCM component carries carbon flux in a living C3 plant.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate biochemical activity in the living recipient plant, rather than only transgene expression or activity in extracted material. Om et al. (2026) reported maize PEPC activity in rice below 2.1% of its in vitro activity; the accessible abstract does not supply sample sizes. This establishes a component result, not coordinated carbon concentration.
milestones.set_by: CCM metabolic-engineering literature, using in vivo function as the component test; the quoted prerequisite was published for C4 rice by Baccolini et al.
milestones.threshold_quote: The ability to measure in vivo flux is a prerequisite for any attempt to engineer a metabolic pathway.

milestones.title: A C3 plant runs four core C4 reactions or forms a Rubisco-containing CCM compartment.
milestones.criterion: A C3 host shows all four core C4 reaction fluxes, or an assembled Rubisco compartment with retained carbon fixation. Reported results: rice, four reactions (5 November 2026; refixation assays, 3 transgenic versus 6 wild-type leaves per point); tobacco, simplified carboxysomes at 2% CO2 (3 September 2018; growth n=4–6 plants), then nine-gene carboxysomes at 1% CO2 (25 April 2023; 3 independent lines); Arabidopsis, proto-pyrenoid condensates (9 December 2020; 3 transgenic lines, gas exchange n=5–8 plants). None establishes a complete CCM.
milestones.set_by: Peer-reviewed CCM reconstruction literature: Baccolini et al. for C4 flux, Long et al. and Chen et al. for carboxysomes, and Atkinson et al. for proto-pyrenoids. Each test is route-specific; the quotation concerns carboxysomes.
milestones.threshold_quote: structural and functional integrity comparable to native carboxysomes

milestones.title: A complete engineered CCM increases CO2 uptake in a living C3 plant.
milestones.criterion: An integrated CCM supplies elevated CO2 to Rubisco, increases carboxylation and suppresses its competing oxygen reaction in a living C3 host. The BBSRC–NSF award targets a functional pyrenoid-based CCM in Arabidopsis, not merely a condensate. The cited rice-flux and compartment-assembly results do not establish this physiological function; Chen et al.'s tobacco could not grow in ambient air.
milestones.set_by: BBSRC–NSF/BIO, award BB/Y000323/1, Technical Summary; published for the pyrenoid route in Arabidopsis. The physiological definition is applied to each mechanism.
milestones.threshold_quote: test a functional pyrenoid-based CCM in Arabidopsis

milestones.title: Field experiments establish an engineered CCM's yield effects in a C3 staple crop.
milestones.criterion: A C3 staple containing the complete CCM undergoes field experiments that establish its yield, product quality, operational efficiency, costs and returns, or resource-quality effects. This is the field-testing branch of USDA's Crop Research TRL 4, following physiological validation. The framework sets no minimum gain, site count, season count or sample size. No field result for a complete engineered CCM in a C3 staple was identified.
milestones.set_by: USDA NIFA, Crop Research Technology Readiness Level, Table 1, TRL 4. Published for supplemental crops, alfalfa/forage and potato programmes; used here as a general crop-testing stage. The criterion appears only in a table.

not_found: No published acceptance test for transfer of a complete CCM between C3 staple species was found.
No field trial of a complete engineered CCM in a C3 staple, or transfer of one between staples, was found.
The Om et al. PubMed page returned no scientific text, and publisher access failed; its sample sizes could not be recovered.
The Baccolini et al. full text was blocked by a cookie redirect and its repository PDF by access controls; the institutional abstract and indexed figure captions were accessible.

results.finding: Maize PEPC in rice showed in planta activity below 2.1% of in vitro activity; sample size not stated.
results.detail: In planta activity was estimated using 13CO2 labeling. The result establishes component activity, not a coordinated CCM.
results.quote: Both cDNAlines and gDNAlines showed higher PEPC activities than wild-type rice, but in planta activity was <2.1% of in vitro activity.

results.finding: Transgenic rice showed up to 10-fold higher PEPC flux than wild type; pulse assays used 3 plants per point for the new lines.
results.detail: The estimate came from labelled malate and aspartate after a 13CO2 pulse. It establishes in vivo component activity.

results.finding: Transgenic rice showed flux through all 4 core C4 reactions; refixation assays used 3 transgenic and 6 wild-type leaves per point.
results.detail: Fluxes were low and measured with sensitive assays, including feeding detached leaves. The study did not establish a complete functional CCM.
results.quote:
We demonstrate that these four core C
4
reactions are operating in rice, establishing the in vivo flux framework needed to progress towards a functional carbon-concentrating mechanism.

results.finding: Three transgenic tobacco lines carried carbon fixation using introduced carboxysomes at 1% CO2.
results.detail: Autotrophic growth showed activity in living plants; the engineered carboxysomes replaced the endogenous Rubisco large subunit.
results.quote:
Nevertheless, the growth of transgenic plants at 1% CO
2
indicated that the catalytic activities of the heterologously engineered α-carboxysomes in tobacco chloroplasts could support plant photosynthesis.

results.finding: Three transgenic tobacco lines formed Rubisco-containing carboxysomes that supported photosynthesis at 1% CO2.
results.detail: The plants could not grow in ambient air; the carboxysomes were not a complete engineered CCM.
results.quote:
Nevertheless, the growth of transgenic plants at 1% CO
2
indicated that the catalytic activities of the heterologously engineered α-carboxysomes in tobacco chloroplasts could support plant photosynthesis.

results.finding: Introduced cyanobacterial Rubisco supported autotrophic growth in tobacco at 2% CO2; growth n=4–6 plants.
results.detail: The transformed plants depended on introduced Form-1A Rubisco. Elevated CO2 was supplied externally; this does not establish a complete CCM.
results.quote:
This minimal gene set produces carboxysomes, which encapsulate the introduced Rubisco and enable autotrophic growth at elevated CO
2
.

results.finding: Tobacco formed Rubisco-containing simplified carboxysomes and grew at 2% CO2; growth n=4–6 plants.
results.detail: The structures lacked carbonic anhydrase and other components needed for full functionality; the plants also lacked the bicarbonate transporters needed for a working CCM.
results.quote:
This minimal gene set produces carboxysomes, which encapsulate the introduced Rubisco and enable autotrophic growth at elevated CO
2
.

results.finding: Arabidopsis proto-pyrenoid condensates contained 54% of Rubisco (n=37 chloroplast images), with retained carbon fixation.
results.detail: Three transgenic lines formed condensates; CO2 assimilation was similar to that of segregant controls. Additional components are needed for a functional carbon-concentrating mechanism.
results.quote:
Immunogold analysis
of chloroplast TEM images from S2 Cr plants expressing EPYC1-
dGFP showed approximately half (54%) of all Rubisco was
contained within the condensate (Figs. 3d, e and Supplementary
Fig. 3b).

results.finding: Arabidopsis proto-pyrenoids retained CO2 assimilation in 3 transgenic lines, with 5–8 rosettes measured per line.
results.detail: The Rubisco-containing condensates were surrounded by starch granules. Photosynthetic parameters were comparable under ambient and 2% oxygen; the authors report no evidence that the starch ring impeded CO2 diffusion.
results.quote:
The photosynthetic 
parameters derived from the A:Ci curves were comparable 
between plants measured under photorespiratory (ambient O2) or 
nonphotorespiratory (2% O2) conditions (SI Appendix, Figs. S10 
and S11), which indicated that the observed growth phenotype 
was not due to reduced Rubisco activity.
